segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two, The Heels on the Bus. So a test of whether or not you are a good guy, it can happen anywhere, as Mike Birbiglia well knows. He's a comedian and told this story onstage in New York.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: Last week, I was meeting my wife in the city for dinner. And I went down to take the subway. And one of the unfortunate things about living in New York with the subway-- and you guys probably know this-- is sometimes on the weekends, the subway is just off.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: And there'll just be a sign that's just like, there isn't the subway, you know? And it'll say, you could take the bus, you know? It's written in pencil. And there's an ellipses, you know?

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: So last weekend, that happened. And so I walked up to the bus. And I said to the bus driver, hey, the subway is off, but it said that I could take the bus to the subway. Do you know where I can get off? And the bus driver said to me, and I quote, he goes, "I don't know anything about the subway."

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: I was like, you don't know anything about the subway? You're wearing the same outfit as the man running the subway. If someone said to me, you see that guy walking down the street with the khaki shorts and the Kings of Leon T-shirt? You know anything about that guy? I'd be like, yeah, I'll tell you a few things about that guy. I know that he could use somebody.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: There's only one other person on the bus. And it's this guy. And he looked up at me, and he goes, I'm taking the subway. You can follow me. So now I'm in an action film. I'm like, got it. I sit down, and I'm following this guy.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: And then we go a few stops. And this lady walks onto the bus. And she was a pretty lady. And she wasn't just bus pretty. Like, she was pretty for the world.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: And I did this thing that I sometimes do when I see a pretty lady, which is I looked at her long enough to realize that she was pretty. And then I looked at the floor. And then I never looked up again. That's my move.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: And so I'm looking at the floor. And then I'm looking up at this guy I'm about to follow, because he's, like, my ride. But then he was staring at the lady. And I know we're all guilty of staring at some point or another. I think we've all done it.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: But I think that there's an etiquette to staring. I think that you can use your peripheral vision if you want to look at somebody. You can stare at someone like you're inside of a spooky painting in Scooby-Doo where your face doesn't move, but then your eyes pan side to side, like you're living in the walls of a mansion.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: But this guy was not doing the spooky painting. He was just full-on staring at this lady like a gargoyle. And I was so mad. I was just like, we all want to stare at the lady. But we don't. Because we are decent people. And we have decided as a group that we are not going to stare at the pretty lady.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: But that's the difference between decent people and creepy people. Creepy people do the things that decent people want to do but have decided are probably not a great idea. Decent people are like, I would like to stare at that pretty lady, but it will make her feel uncomfortable. Creepy people are like, look, I'm going for it.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: We go a few more stops, and the creepy guy stands up, looks at me, and says, let's go. I was like, oh great. Now she thinks I'm with you. This pretty lady and I have built up a rapport where we have an understanding that she is pretty and I am decent. And when I am in her presence, I stare at the floor. And now she thinks I am with you, a creepy man.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: And so as I walk by this woman, I try to convey all of this with my eyes. Like, I am not with this guy. And that look takes so long to convey that the look itself becomes creepy. And I know it. And so I say, sorry, which were the first words uttered in a conversation we were not having.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: As this woman understands her bus ride, she walked onto a bus, a creepy man stared at her for 10 minutes and then left the bus, and then another man, who she did not know was on the bus, approached her and apologized, which means what he did is worse.

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: And I'm so frustrated about the unfairness of the situation that when I get to the dinner with my wife, I'm explaining this whole thing in detail. And I'm like, it's not fair, because I am not creepy. I am decent. And my wife says, wait, is the moral of the story that you want credit for just not being creepy?

segments.speaker: Mike Birbiglia
segments.text: And I was like, exactly. Because I think that decent people are undervalued. And my wife says, but you do get credit. I married you. And I said, I want more than that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today on our program-- good guys, stories of people trying to be good guys and not always sure if they're succeeding.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We have arrived at Act Three of our program. Act Three, No Man Left Behind. We now turn to a kind of classic story of a buddy who's trying to do a solid for another guy from Julia DeWitt.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Out in the desert scrublands of northern South Africa in a place called The Karoo, there's nothing-- no trees, no water-- for as far as you can see.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: You're in a primeval landscape.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: This is Don Shirley. Why he knows this place so well will become clear in a minute.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: You see a little rise. And when you get to the little hill, there's actually a big hollow there where the ground has collapsed. At the bottom of a very steep slope, you actually have a sheer face in front of you.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: And at the bottom of this sheer face is a puddle. So you think, oh, this is just a little puddle that doesn't go anywhere. But when you take the duck weed off the top, it's actually clear water.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Which means that this isn't just standing water. This water is filtering down to somewhere.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: Now, if you go into this puddle, there's a small slot that goes through, which is just wide enough for a man's body to go through. After 20 foot, you're now starting to enter the cave, and gradually the cave gets wider.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Down below you is 900 feet of water. This is Bushman's Cave.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: It's a huge cave. Now, if you take the Eiffel Tower and stand it on the floor of Bushman's Cave, the top of the tower would be just about coming out of the water.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: The cave is almost 1,000 feet deep and 2 and 1/2 football fields wide. The main thing that lives in the pitch darkness is a species of strange little blind white cave shrimp. Otherwise, the cave is dark, deep, and dead. This cave is a dangerous place for humans. And it's basically totally inaccessible to almost all of us. But for deep water divers, this is heaven.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: There are only a very few divers on the planet that have ever been anywhere near the bottom of this cave. And only about a dozen recreational divers ever dive to these kinds of depths, period. Don is one of these extreme divers. He met another of these deep water divers, a guy named Dave Shaw, back in 2002. They were immediately friends. And a couple of years later, Don took Dave to dive Bushman's.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: On dive day, they got to the puddle, and Dave went in first. Dave swam down through the slot, and the cave opened up below him. While he was going down, he was doing something called laying a shot line. Basically, he was leaving a trail of rope in the total darkness. This is the only way he knew how to get out of the cave.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: You're in pitch black, absolute pitch black. So if you shined a light in any direction, it would disappear. The darkness will eat the light. Basically, being 900 foot in a cave, you might as well be on the Moon. In fact, I think more people have walked on the Moon than have actually been to those sorts of depths in caves.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: This sounds unbelievable, but it's true. More people have been on the Moon than have been to the depths that these guys have. Now, Dave was exploring on the bare floor of the cavern. There's nothing to see but his light in the black and the white rope that he dragged with him. Then suddenly--

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: His torch caught the remains of Deon Dreyer.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: No one knows exactly what happened to Deon Dreyer. But a decade earlier, Deon was diving with a team in Bushman's. When they stopped to take a headcount, Deon was gone. People had been looking for his body ever since.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: He was still in his wetsuit, still wearing his cylinders-- a collection of bones inside a wetsuit. And at the time, he tried to move the body. But the body was stuck in the silt. He was panting, and he said, I shouldn't work hard at this depth. It wasn't in the plan. So I needed to leave the body there.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Deon was 20 when he was lost in Bushman's. Dave didn't take finding Deon lightly.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: He thought of it more of a mission to actually-- his task to bring this body back.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: So when Dave came up, he told Don he was going to come back and get Deon's body.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: He phoned up Deon's parents and said, I'm going to retrieve your son's body.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: The thing is that a dive like this is a major operation. It took them months to plan.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: You're at 900 foot under the water. There's a lot of risk involved in that. Every 33 foot that you go down effectively doubles the risk. When you're down at those depths, anything that goes wrong is an issue.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Combining extreme depths with the hard work that Dave had to do to get Deon's body into a body bag came with a lot of risk. At depth, too much nitrogen is kind of like a narcotic. Basically, it feels suddenly like you drank five martinis in a row.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Too much helium can give you twitching fits. If you breathe too heavily, like Dave might have to while he's moving around Deon's body, you pass out. And then, of course, there's the bends.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: If you come too quickly, it's like opening a Coke bottle once you've shook it up. And it fizzes. And then, you would have problems with bubbles in your blood.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: To prevent the bends, Dave would take several hours to come up to the surface. So they recruited a team of support divers that would go into the water intervals to check on Dave at various depths while he came up.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: And the rule was, no one will go deeper than the depth where we actually plan for them to be.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don would go the deepest.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: But as far as Dave and I were concerned, basically what we said is if Dave has a problem, he would signal me. And in caving, when you flash a light, you wave a light around, that's a distress signal.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: We got to the day that we're actually planning to do the main dive. And we went down early in the morning. It was still dark. The sun was not quite up yet. And at 6:15, Dave went under the water. I followed 14 minutes later.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don followed the shot line down through the slot and into the cave.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: So as I was going down, falling through this black space, I was expecting to see some rising bubbles as I was going down. Also I would see Dave's light where he was coming back. When I was going down, I didn't actually see any bubbles coming back. What I did see-- in the area where I thought he would actually be, I did see a light. It was one light, a solid light just shining.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: But the light wasn't moving.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: Something is not quite right. And he's spending longer doing something. And then I knew that I would probably be going down to the bottom.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don dove past 800 feet, deeper than he had ever been before.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: Now, I went past my target depth. But the problem was, as I got to 833 foot, I actually had my own personal problems go on then.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: He heard a sharp crack.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: My rebreather controller actually imploded.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: This just means a piece of his breathing apparatus broke. Don trained constantly for moments like this. So he knew exactly what to do. He would just add oxygen to his gas mixture manually.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: But at that sort of depth, any oxygen that you add makes a hell of a difference. And I pushed my oxygen pressure much too high inadvertently. Now, that's very unhealthy at that depth-- very unhealthy. So now, I was liable to actually pass out very quickly.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don knew then that this was it. It was the end of the line. He had to turn around and go back.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: The surface is not somewhere that you can actually go to solve a problem. When you have a problem, you have to solve that problem there where you are. And if you don't solve that problem, you don't come back. You have to put the brakes on, as it were, at that point. And I was thinking, OK, Dave might come back. He's either dead, or he's working his way back. But all I could deal with was what was in front of me.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don knew that he now had over 10 hours in the water ahead of him. Don slowly ascended up to the roof of the cave. At this point, he started to pass out. And then, he got a helium bubble in his ear.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: And that made me lose balance completely. I'm over this extreme depth of water. You then have no-- absolutely no-- sense of up, down, sideways, or anything. And I didn't really have any sense of really where I was.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don lost grip on the shot line. And as he was passing out, reviving again, and passing out, he started swimming in these little circles, spinning around looking for the line. Remember, this line is the only way Don knows how to get out of the cave.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: And I'm in this void, the black. I had an extremely bright light in my hand. And where the light was going into the black, I was seeing black. And where the light was hitting the roof, I was seeing light, white. And then, I'd keep spinning around like that. So I was seeing black, white, black, white, black, white.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: And then, I caught the line, the white line, in my torch. And the next time I spun around, I grabbed hold of the line. The trouble was, now I had vertigo. And that makes you vomit, right? So now, I was vomiting underwater as well, vomiting in between breaths, effectively. As time went on, I couldn't breathe anymore.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don eventually stabilized himself. And he started his ascent again towards the surface. He met a support diver. And using a waterproof pencil and one of these slates the divers use to communicate underwater, Don wrote him a message.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: I said, I'm OK, and Dave's not coming back. But still, in my mind, I had a hope that he would. From that point on, the guys had a task, which was to support me.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: For hours, the team up above waited to see if he would make it out alive. His only job was to breathe. Dave's light down below had disappeared.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: If you see the videos of me coming up, you would think, this guy's half-dead. It had been just over 12 hours in the water. I couldn't actually really do much for myself other than breathe. My head was like a marshmallow.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Don was put into a decompression chamber and then taken in the morning for more treatment at a hospital in Johannesburg. Dave did not come up that night. Dave was dead. And then, a week later, Don got some news.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: I actually was told that Dave's body had come up. During that week, there'd been lots of speculation as to what had happened. Dave was carrying a camera on his head. In retrieving the camera, then we could piece together really what happened.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: As the camera rolls, you see Dave trying to get Deon's body into a body bag.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: One of his lights had actually got tangled up in the line and smashed. So now, bearing in mind you're in the pitch black, his main light had actually been broken. So he couldn't really see so well.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Then Dave also gets tangled. He pulls away. But now he's tied to Deon's body.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: And you could see that he was working trying to get himself out of this line. He was cutting with the scissors. But his scissors weren't even getting anywhere near the line.

segments.speaker: Julia Dewitt
segments.text: Listening to the video, you can hear Dave's breathing start to get shallower and shallower as he starts working harder and harder.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: Dave passed out from too much carbon dioxide. He worked right up-- right up-- to the very last breath that he ever took trying to get out. And then the camera just carries on recording until the batteries run out.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: There's barely a day goes by where I don't think of Dave. And really, there are a lot of times I turn around-- I do a fantastic dive, and I just want to say, did you see that? And Dave very much did die nobly doing what he did. He did everything that he should do.

segments.speaker: Don Shirley
segments.text: And he died, as they'd say in the military, with his boots on. When Dave's body had come up, hanging underneath Dave's body, cocooned in the line that Dave originally had laid, was Deon Dreyer's body. So Dave actually achieved what he wanted to do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That story came from Julia DeWitt. That was first broadcast on the Public Radio show Snap Judgment , which has gotten so good. If you are not downloading their podcast every week already, it's at snapjudgment.org or the iTunes store. They're also heard on many Public Radio stations.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Four, The Deepest, Darkest Open Secret. More than four years ago, back in 2009, a US soldier got in touch with our program. And he was attached to a special operations combat unit. He was getting ready to deploy to Afghanistan.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he offered to do a story for us about what it's really like to serve. One of our program's producers, Sarah Koenig, started talking to him. His one condition is that we would not use his name. So for this story that you're about to hear, we're calling him Adam, which is a pseudonym that he chose.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And a disclaimer-- Adam says some disturbing things about himself, but also about his fellow soldiers. We want to be clear that this is just his own experience. This is his own thoughts. This is his own perspective, his own story. He does not speak for the military in general. He is speaking for himself.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We think also that this story about war probably is not something that children should be hearing. And a warning-- also we quote some people who use an offensive term at one point in the story. OK, here's Sarah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: When he first got in touch with us, Adam said he wasn't like the other guys in the Army. For one thing, he was almost 30 when he joined, about a decade older than most people. And he'd had a good career in the tech world as an engineer. But he had been unhappy doing that. He wanted to try something difficult and frightening and unknown.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: He decided he wanted to go to war, even though he thought the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq were bogus and even though the other guys in his unit considered him-- and this is their language-- a "liberal fagot." So yeah, he said he'd give us an outsider's perspective. And I said, sure, let's see what happens. So he started sending me recordings from Afghanistan like installments in a diary. And then, not too long after he deployed, Adam sent me a recording I found jarring.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: In infantry school, I would be shocked of the reasons that people were there. People-- well, I wouldn't say "people." Men want to kill other young men. That's why they were there.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: It seemed to Adam that the way they talked about it, a lot of macho bluster about wanting to kill the bad guys, was just a cover for a much more basic desire they had-- that deep down, these guys didn't want to just kill the enemy. They wanted the opportunity to kill another human being period.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Not everyone was like this, he said, but most of them. And at first, Adam said, this kind of disturbed him. But then, after a while, it didn't.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: So I've really realized, building up to my deployment, that I'm not any different than most of these people. Regardless of the noble aspirations I say I have for joining the army, I'm pretty sure I just want the opportunity to kill someone too. If I'm being honest with myself, it's there.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Take a moment to compile all your stereotypes of a Public Radio producer. And now apply them to me. And you're right. I'm exactly who you think I am. I'm a peaceful sort. I don't come from a military family. I've not been in a lot of bar fights. I haven't lived in the South, playing violent video games.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: That makes me very different from Adam, who did all those things. So I recognize I'm coming to this a little more wide-eyed than a lot of other people might. Still, I don't know what to make of Adam. I like him. I like talking to him. I think he's smart and weird and honest.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Here's a rational man saying he wants to kill someone just to see what that's like. What are we supposed to make of that? But this isn't a story where I'm going to get to the bottom of that question in the next 15 or 20 minutes. This is a story where I just ask that you hear him out.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Some things you should know before we start-- Adam ended up doing three different tours in Afghanistan between 2009 and 2011. And he never did kill anyone. Being in war messed him up in certain ways. He's been seeing psychologists weekly for a couple of years. He's been diagnosed with severe PTSD. He has dramatic mood swings. And he barely sleeps, maybe three or four hours a night.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Adam's not on active duty anymore. He's back in the US working on a Ph.D. And so recently I played him back some of the recordings he'd sent me. I wanted to find out what he made of his 2009 self.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And he said, yeah, what I said back then about wanting to kill someone, that wasn't an exaggeration. And it had surprised him to realize it, he said, because he was in his late 20s when he joined. He thought he knew himself pretty well. But the army and the training, it changed him.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: You do learn to-- they do teach you to want that. You yearn for that in basic training, or at least infantry basic training. Just over and over again, the only success you ever have is hitting a target or winning a fight in basic training.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Everything else you do you're criticized for. But if you do those things, you're doing good. And the interaction you have with the drill sergeant, most of it is based on killing somebody.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I want to play you another piece of tape. It's when you get some prisoners that you're in charge of. OK. Here, I'm going to play it.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: We recently just rolled up two high-valued targets. And we didn't kill them. We captured them. And we brought them back to base.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: And we have a temporary holding facility-- temporary jail, really-- where we kept them until they could be transferred to Bagram. And while they were being held here, which was like three days, we had to rotate shifts just to guard them. It's just a basic sit outside their cell, make sure that they don't hang themselves type of thing.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: And at least two other people came up to me and said it was really hard for them not to shoot them while they were in the cell. Now, don't get me wrong. One of these guys was a Taliban leader, and another guy was his little deputy. These were bad people.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: But they were really nice. I mean, personal interactions with them-- I felt bad for them. Because they're crying. They miss their families. They were very polite.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: But even I wanted to shoot them, even though they were unarmed, behind bars, uncombative. Something-- it's not a revenge thing. It's not a hey, you killed a bunch of my buddies thing, hey, you're a threat to society thing.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: It's a hey, I want to shoot you, because I want to know what it's like, what it feels like to shoot you. It sounds sick. But it's probably much more prevalent than most people care to believe.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Um-- do you remember that?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: No. It's completely accurate. I remember feeling those things. I don't remember that specific situation, just because I can't remember those specific people. But that's just because that situation happened so many times.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah. More times than I can count. Half the people we rolled up were probably innocent. But we would have killed them all if we could have got away with it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But see, that really sounds just homicidal, like straight-up homicidal.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: That is straight-up homicidal. It was simply fear of repercussions that stopped those people from being murdered.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And you're saying that was the norm?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah, this is not an abnormal mindset.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: How do you know that's not abnormal?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Because I've been around hundreds of men that have the same mindset. This is not me. I am merely a representative of the community that I was working in.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And you're saying that's because these are the enemy, and they're going to kill us, and so--

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: That's-- I mean, people can say it in those terms. But it's not like that. It's very much-- you have the power to do it. And you're on the verge of having the permission to do it. So you want to do it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So it's just more primal than that, you're saying.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I have to say, before you talked about this, I had never heard anybody say this, really.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Say?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: That I wanted to go kill somebody and admit it.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah, I've never heard anybody say it either.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: (LAUGHING) And so I can't tell if he's just crazy, or if he's the bravest bastard out there. And he's just willing to admit something that nobody else will admit.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I would say there's probably no chance that I am on one side of that spectrum or the other. It is probably somewhere in between. I can't give you an accurate estimate of which spectrum I fall closer to.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, so you don't know yourself?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I've seen four psychologists in the last 24 months. No, I don't know if I'm crazy. Some people seem to think so.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Was it a situation where-- at this point, you're saying you're a few months in-- where every day you were kind of thinking, I wonder if today's the day I'm going to shoot someone? I wonder if today's the day.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Every day, yes. Every day-- every mission we went out on, I was hoping I'd get to shoot somebody. This was actively talked about. Everybody wanted to get their first kill. Not everybody-- many people already had their first kill. But if you didn't have your first kill yet, everybody was talking about, OK, is this the day you're going to get your first kill?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Because people know when you have it?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: It's a thing?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Of course they know. But if you do have a kill, people have a greater amount of trust in you. People know you're dependable. People know that you're willing to cross that threshold. And there's just some benefits to that.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Because you've been tested, kind of?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The next piece of tape I want to play you, it's about being on a mission one night and having the opportunity to shoot at someone. Do you remember how long you'd been there at this point when this happened? Do you have a memory of this?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I remember in detail everything about this situation.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: OK, how long had you been in Afghanistan when this happened?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: A few months.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: A few months, OK. And up until that point, it seems like you had sort of indirectly caused the deaths of people by kind of sighting people, and those guys got killed. But it was indirect, is that right?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I had shot at people. And I knew those people that I shot at died. But everybody was shooting at them. So I have no idea if I shot them. And I called out targets to aircraft.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: OK, so let me play this. Here we go.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: It's almost 1 o'clock on Sunday, November 8. It's the day after a mission. And if my voice sounds a little weird, it's because I'm on a lot of drugs. It was night, last night, and we were coming down to land. And apparently the pilot thought the ground was actually 50 to 100 feet lower than it actually was. So we came slamming into the ground pretty hard. And I hurt my back pretty good-- nothing structural, just some muscle.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: But anyway, the worst part about this mission was I was on a security element. So people breached the door and went in there and looked for bad guys and stuff. I'm looking for bad guys out in fields and around the buildings, just trying to make sure nobody's coming to get us.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: But I actually saw-- it's late at this point. There shouldn't be anybody awake walking around. And I actually saw a guy. And so this guy pops up in my sites. And I want to shoot him, but I didn't. He didn't have a gun, and he wasn't coming towards me. But I knew he was a bad guy. And I still didn't shoot him.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I don't know what that says about me. I don't know if it means that I'm either afraid to kill somebody or just that I want to kill somebody for the right reasons. Or maybe it just means I'm a puss, and I hesitate to pull the trigger.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Do you remember that incident?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Oh yeah, vividly.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: What do you think about it now?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I still would have shot that guy. Well, I know a lot more about that guy now. He turned out to be a very bad guy. So I definitely would have shot him on sight.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Why do you think you didn't?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I think I was still worried about the repercussions of shooting somebody that was unarmed.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Repercussions meaning just sort of morally to yourself or that you could actually get in trouble with your superiors or something?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah, there would actually-- I thought there might be some trouble with my superiors, which there would not have been.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Right. But you're saying in the tape, maybe I just want to shoot someone for the right reasons, or I don't want to shoot somebody who's unarmed. Or maybe I'm just a puss. You seem to be questioning more than that.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah, I was. I was wondering if those were actually the reasons. They are not.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: What do you mean? How do you know?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I've thought about it for about three years and five months.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And so you never did kill anyone.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: No. I messed some people up, but I never killed them.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And how do you feel about that?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Um-- yeah, I think I missed the boat on that one, missed my opportunity to do that. I think the opportunity to kill somebody in the United States, to have the experience of taking another life, is going to be pretty slim unless I want to go to jail or a mental institution.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But I'm never hearing you say, it's just wrong to kill other people. You're not saying that.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Is it wrong to kill other people?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I think it is.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Regardless of motive?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: No, I guess not regardless of motive. But it is wrong to kill someone for the experience of killing them.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Yeah. So yeah, I would say maybe it is a bit sociopathic. I wouldn't change how I characterize it at all, though. I would say that my threshold for violence is much lower now. And I would kill people in situations much more readily or much more quickly than the normal person would. And I actively hope to have those situations.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Do you think you're seeking them out?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Am I putting myself in those situations?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Yeah, like getting in bar fights or something where somebody could get killed.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: No. I mean, I started drinking quite a bit there for a while. I have got into some confrontations with some less than polite people. My temper is very short if somebody was to be impolite or rude to me. I don't go around looking at people and saying, I want to kill them. But if I have a good excuse to kill somebody, I'd definitely take that opportunity. I would-- yeah, I think I would.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I mean, is this what you're largely discussing with psychologists? I mean--

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Are they hearing this and having the reaction I'm having, or no?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: They don't hear any of this. They want to talk about my mother, for God's sakes.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, you're not talking to them about this?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I literally-- I tried to guide them there at first. But now, they just really want to talk about my relationship with my mother.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, for real-- like, you're not saying it as a cliche. Like, actually they're trying to talk about your mother.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: No, it's not a cliche. It's true. This is absolutely true.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But it doesn't also sound like you're worried about this impulse in yourself.

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: Why would I be worried?

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I don't know. Because what if you end up killing somebody?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: That is entirely possible, yes.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But why aren't you worried about that?

segments.speaker: Adam
segments.text: I don't know. It just never crossed my mind that I wouldn't be able to justify it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I spoke to other men who trained with Adam and who also served in Afghanistan doing the same job as Adam's. And I asked them if it was real, this mindset of wanting to kill just to kill. And they all said, yeah. Maybe not to the extent Adam experienced it, but yeah. They said it was common.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: They said things like, quote, "It's not pretty to talk about. And nobody wants to hear that back home. But that's part of it." Another guy said, "I didn't join to go out and kill people. But once you do the training, I don't know, it's almost like a job. And your job is to kill people. And you do want that experience."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I talked to a psychiatric expert on war trauma and PTSD. And he also agreed. "This is true," he said. "This is a part of war that people like to ignore, the pleasure of killing. Killing is our society's most basic prohibition. So that's what military training is for," he said, "to get people to the point where they can cross that line."

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Of course, the US military doesn't want sociopaths or would-be murderers in its ranks. Doctor Michael Matthews, a psychology professor at West Point who studies how soldiers react in dangerous situations, said in his experience, soldiers who truly think that way, who really just want to kill for killing's sake, those people are uncommon. And if they do surface, he said, they should be screened and probably kicked out of the military, which Adam would agree with.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But what Adam is saying is that there's a subtler thing that happens. There's some other class of people who aren't sociopaths but who go through military training, and the desire to kill is suddenly there. It seems natural to him that this happens, normal. But just because bloodlust is normal, that doesn't mean Adam thinks it's OK. In fact, he thinks he shouldn't have been allowed to go to Afghanistan at all.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sarah Koenig is one of the producers of our show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
